title: The match statement
learningGoals: choose between exact values with match and case

youtube.description: In this episode you will choose between exact values with match and case, combine values with the | symbol and add case _ as the catch-all, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Match and case · 0:54 A menu with match · 1:34 The value being matched · 2:06 Second program · 3:06 Recap · 3:37 Bug of the Day · 4:25 Challenge · 4:45 Next episode

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: When one value can be one of many exact options, an elif ladder gets long. Today we meet a tidier tool, match.

scenes.onScreen: "Match and case": three numbered lines (1. match looks at one value; 2. Each case is a pattern to compare with; 3. case _ catches everything else) and an analogy card: a restaurant menu: you say the dish number, and the kitchen picks the matching dish
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: The match statement looks at one value, and compares it with a list of cases. The first case that fits runs. Think of a restaurant menu. You say the dish number, and the kitchen picks the matching dish. You can join several values with a vertical bar, meaning, or. And case underscore is the catch-all. It matches anything that nothing else matched. It needs Python three ten or newer.

lines: Each case is a pattern to compare with

analogy.title: Think of it like this
analogy.body: a restaurant menu: you say the dish number, and the kitchen picks the matching dish

scenes.onScreen: menu.py: a dish number matched to a dish
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right; faint indent guide lines
scenes.narration: [HL 1] Choice is two. [HL 2] Match looks at the value of choice. [HL 3] Case one compares. Not a match. [HL 4] Skipped. [HL 5] Case two matches. [HL 6] So Prawn rice prints. [HL 7] Case underscore is the catch-all. It matches any other number. [HL 8] Not on the menu prints for it. Match stops at the first case that fits.

code.source:
choice = 2
match choice:
    case 1:
        print("Fish curry")
    case 2:
        print("Prawn rice")
    case _:
        print("Not on the menu")

scenes.onScreen: The name choice tied to the int 2
scenes.animation: Name tags pop in with their arrows to the objects (value and type shown, no addresses); when Python reads a name the arrow glows and the object lights up
scenes.narration: Match does not change anything in memory. The name choice stays tied to the int two. Match only looks at the object, and compares it with each pattern in order. Nothing is created and nothing is tied by the cases here. It works just like an elif ladder with double equals, but it reads better.

scenes.onScreen: day.py: Sat or Sun is Weekend
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 1] [TRACK day=Sat] The day is the text Sat. [HL 2] Match the day. [HL 3] One case can hold several patterns joined with a vertical bar. Read it as, Sat or Sun. [HL 4] Weekend prints. [HL 5] The catch-all for every other day. [HL 6] Weekday. With one case instead of two, the program is shorter and clearer.

code.source:
day = "Sat"
match day:
    case "Sat" | "Sun":
        print("Weekend")
    case _:
        print("Weekday")

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the command types with key-tick, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as day dot py. In the terminal, type python, space, day dot py. Weekend.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One: match compares one value with a list of cases. Two: The first matching case runs and the rest are skipped. Three: A vertical bar joins several patterns in one case. Four: case _ catches everything that nothing else matched. Pause the video, and say these ideas out loud, once, slowly.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: no case underscore
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. The command is jump. No case matches it. And there is no catch-all. So match does nothing at all. No error, no message, just silence. Silent failures are the hardest to find. Add case underscore at the end, with a friendly message, and unknown commands are handled.

props.wrongCode:
command = "jump"
match command:
    case "start":
        print("Starting")
    case "stop":
        print("Stopping")
props.fixedCode:
command = "jump"
match command:
    case "start":
        print("Starting")
    case "stop":
        print("Stopping")
    case _:
        print("Unknown command")
props.why: If no case fits and there is no case _, match does nothing and gives no error, so a wrong input fails silently.

shorts.title: What is match?
shorts.hook: "Match is a tidy way to choose between exact values."
shorts.script: Match is a tidy way to choose between exact values. You write match, then a value. Below it, each case shows a pattern to compare with. The first case that fits runs, and the others are skipped. Think of a restaurant menu. You say the dish number, and the kitchen picks the dish. It needs Python three ten or newer, and it reads like a menu. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: A menu for your code.

shorts.title: The catch-all
shorts.script: Case underscore is the catch-all. It matches any value that no earlier case matched. Put it last. Without it, a value that fits no case does nothing, and shows no error. With it, you can print a friendly message, such as, not on the menu. Every match statement should end with a catch-all, just as every elif ladder should end with an else. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: End with case underscore.

shorts.title: Or inside a case
shorts.hook: "A case can match several values at once."
shorts.script: A case can match several values at once. Join them with a vertical bar, which reads as or. Case Sat bar Sun matches both weekend days. So one case does the work of two. Your program gets shorter and easier to read. Use the bar whenever several values should give the same result, and avoid repeating yourself. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: One case, many values.

shorts.title: Silent failure
shorts.script: A tricky bug. You match a command, but the command is not in your list, and you forgot the catch-all. Python does nothing. No error, no message, just silence. Silent failures are the hardest bugs to find. The fix is easy. Add case underscore at the end, with a friendly message. Always plan for unexpected input, from real users. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Plan for the unexpected.
